toc.title: Edit and Adapt for the Audience

html:
1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. HTML: hypertext markup language; AI: artificial intelligence

  • How to edit and adapt Claude's output for a specific audience
  • How to compare versions and refine them
  • How to organize and curate information
  • How to choose the right output format: inline, artifact, file or structured data

2Edit and Adapt for the Audience

Running case

Cedarbrook's One Message, Three Readers

  • The operations lead has a technical note: a warehouse system change delays shipments by two days
  • It must go to warehouse staff, customer-care agents and customers
  • Claude adapts the same facts into three versions: an operational checklist, a talking-points sheet and a short, friendly notice

What to adapt Examples of instructions
Tone "Friendly and apologetic", "formal and concise", "neutral and factual"
Reading level "Plain language for a general reader", "explain terms for a new hire"
Length "100 words", "one page", "three bullets"
Detail "Executive summary only", "include the full steps"
Structure "Headline plus three bullets", "numbered procedure", "table"
Language and region "Translate to Spanish, US retail style"; native speakers should review important translations
Voice "Match the style of this example" or a saved style
  • Keep facts fixed and change delivery. Ask Claude to list any facts it changed so you can confirm nothing was altered.
  • Edit like an editor: read for accuracy first, then clarity, then tone. Use targeted instructions ("cut the second paragraph by half").
  • In an artifact such as a document, highlight a passage and ask Claude to edit just that part so the rest stays untouched.
  • Compare versions side by side: ask for two variants, a table of differences, or "which is more suitable for X and why". You choose.
  • You own the final text. Claude's output is a draft; keep your voice and responsibility.
Exam tip

Adapting means same facts, different delivery. If the facts change between versions, that is an error to catch, not an adaptation.

3Organize and Curate Information

Claude is strong at turning messy material into usable structure.

Need Ask Claude to Output
Make sense of notes Group by theme; pull out decisions, risks, actions Headed summary or table
Compare options Build a comparison on stated criteria Table with a row per option
Sort and label Categorize feedback, tickets, survey comments Table with a category column
Remove duplicates and clutter Merge duplicates, drop irrelevant items, keep sources Clean list
Prioritize Rank by your criteria (impact, effort, urgency) and show the reasoning Ranked list
Extract fields Pull names, dates, amounts from documents Table or CSV-style list
Create a knowledge base Turn FAQs and policies into a clean, consistent document Document for a Project (Module 11)
  • Curate means choose and shape, not just collect: decide what the reader needs, cut the rest, and cite the source of each item.
  • For extraction and sorting, spot-check rows against the originals, because a missed or misread row is easy to overlook (Module 4).

4Choosing the Output Format

Format Use when Notes
Inline (in the chat) A quick answer, a short draft, an explanation Fast; disappears into the thread
Artifact Substantial, self-contained content you will edit, reuse or share: documents, slides, designs, small interactive tools, dashboards, diagrams Opens beside the chat; lives in the Artifacts tab; editable; private by default; share on purpose
File (Excel, Word, PowerPoint, PDF) You need a standard file for colleagues or other tools Needs Create and edit files (code execution) turned on; download or save to Drive
Structured data The output will feed another tool or sheet: table, CSV, list with fixed fields, JSON-like format State the exact columns or fields
  • Claude tends to create an artifact when content is significant and self-contained (roughly over 15 lines), likely to be edited or reused, understandable without the chat and worth coming back to.
  • Artifact types and templates include Docs, Slides, Design, Dashboards (beta) and small interactive tools [Verify live]. Docs export to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs; decks export to PowerPoint or PDF; designs to PDF, PowerPoint or HTML.
  • Artifacts start private. Sharing controls who can open them. Treat artifacts from unknown sources with caution because they bring someone else's code into your chat.
  • An artifact error can be sent back with "Try fixing with Claude"; success is not guaranteed.
  • AI-powered artifacts (small apps that call Claude) use the viewer's own Claude account and plan limits.
  • Artifacts can store data (personal or shared, text only, small limit). Check whether storage is shared before putting sensitive information in.
  • For structured data, name the format and fields: "Return a table with columns Name, Date, Amount, Source" and then check the rows.
Exam tip

"Which format?" questions turn on reuse and audience. Reusable, editable, shareable content: artifact or file. One-off answer: inline. Data for another tool: structured.

Exam tip

A targeted edit of one passage beats regenerating the whole document: it keeps what is good and saves usage.

5Exam Q&A

S1A coordinator must send the same shipping delay notice to warehouse staff and to customers. What is the best approach?

  • ASend the same technical note to both groups unchanged and let each reader work out what matters
  • BWrite different facts for each group
  • CAsk Claude to adapt the same facts for each audience, then check that the facts did not change
  • DAsk Claude to write only the customer version
Show the answer

Answer: C. Adapt tone and detail while keeping facts constant, and verify nothing was altered.

S2A manager has a 20-page product guide and wants a reusable, editable one-page summary to share with the sales team. Which output fits best?

  • AA voice message
  • BA plain text list with no structure that is pasted into an email thread
  • CAn inline reply that disappears into the chat once the conversation moves on
  • DAn artifact or a document file that the team can edit and reuse
Show the answer

Answer: D. Substantial, reusable, shareable content suits an artifact or a file.

S3An analyst needs customer feedback categorized so it can be pasted into a spreadsheet. Which instruction helps most?

  • A"Give me your general impressions of the feedback and what stood out most to you overall."
  • B"Return a table with columns Comment, Category, Sentiment, and the comment ID for each row."
  • C"Write a story about the feedback."
  • D"Summarize the feedback."
Show the answer

Answer: B. Structured data needs stated fields; IDs make spot-checking possible.

S4A user wants to change only the second paragraph of a document Claude produced in an artifact. What is the efficient way?

  • ARegenerate the whole document and hope the rest is unchanged
  • BDelete the artifact and create a brand new one from the original request
  • CHighlight the paragraph and ask Claude to edit just that part
  • DOpen a new chat and start over, pasting in everything that was produced so far
Show the answer

Answer: C. Targeted editing leaves the rest of the artifact untouched.

S5Artifacts are shared with whom by default?

  • AAnyone with the chat link
  • BAll team members
  • CThe whole internet, because artifacts are published by default
  • DNobody; artifacts start private and sharing is a choice
Show the answer

Answer: D. Artifacts start private; sharing controls who can open them.

S6Which TWO are good reasons to choose an artifact over an inline answer? Select TWO.

  • AThe content must disappear after the chat
  • BThe content is a yes-or-no answer
  • CThe content will be edited, reused or shared
  • DThe content is substantial and self-contained
  • EThe content is a short one-sentence reply
Show the answer

Answer: C, D. Artifacts suit significant, self-contained content that people will edit, reuse or share.

S7Claude rewrote a policy summary for customers and the refund window changed from 30 to 14 days. What does this show?

  • AA sign that the policy changed
  • BA factual error introduced during adaptation that must be corrected
  • CGood adaptation of tone
  • DNormal variation in format
Show the answer

Answer: B. Adapting changes tone and detail only, so a changed refund window is an error introduced during rewriting and must be corrected.

S8A team wants to pull supplier names, dates and amounts out of 40 invoices into a table. What should they do after Claude returns the table?

  • ASpot-check rows against the original invoices
  • BAsk Claude if it is sure
  • CDelete the originals
  • DUse it directly in accounting without any further checking
Show the answer

Answer: A. Extraction can miss or misread items, so compare a sample with the source.

S9An artifact built by a colleague asks you to run it. What caution applies?

  • ANone at all; artifacts are always safe to run, whoever created them and however they were shared
  • BDisable your account first
  • CTreat artifacts from unknown sources with caution, because you bring their code into your chat
  • DOnly run it on mobile
Show the answer

Answer: C. Check the source before using an artifact from someone you do not know.

6Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Adapt Same facts; change tone, level, length, detail, structure, language
Edit Accuracy first, then clarity, then tone; highlight a part to edit only that part
Compare Ask for variants or a difference table; you choose
Organize Group, compare, sort, dedupe, prioritize, extract; cite sources; spot-check
Inline Quick answers and short drafts
Artifact Substantial, self-contained, reusable; Artifacts tab; private by default; export to Word, PDF, PowerPoint
File Office or PDF files; needs Create and edit files turned on
Structured data Name columns or fields; verify rows
Caution Untrusted artifacts; shared storage and sensitive data
